newsitem.title: USA: Stocks hit records, dollar little changed.
newsitem.headline: Stocks hit records, dollar little changed.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks shook off early selling pressure and set record highs for the second time in three days Wednesday as investors sought the safety of big companies more likely to deliver solid earnings.
Bonds edged lower and the dollar ended mixed. Crude oil prices fell.
The Dow index of 30 blue chips rose 16.03 points to close at 6,020.81, its 29th record this year, surpassing Monday's 6,010.00, which was its first close above 6,000.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks also set a new high, with a gain of 1.84 points at 704.41, topping Monday's record of 703.54.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances by a narrow margin, 1,212 to 1,124, on heavy volume of 441.4 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"The OTC (over-the-counter) and broad markets are still under pressure with investor nervousness over profit margins in the technology area and a flight to quality," said Michael Metz, Oppenheimer & Co.'s chief investment strategist.
"We had a big run in tech stocks and it looks like investors are turning risk-averse," he said.
Profit-taking in technology stocks drove the Nasdaq composite index down 7.11 points to 1,250.99 after setting two straight record closes Monday and Tuesday.
Peggy Farley, chief executive officer at Amas Securities, said that despite some profit-taking by investors sceptical the market rally can continue, many people were buying on dips.
"You see downturns and recoveries, which indicate that there is buying whenever the market moves down," she said. "There are as many bulls out there, if not more, than there are bears."
Farley said sellers were motivated by profit-taking rather than a rush into cash, something evident in the modest nature of the market's decline.
"There are very few players who anticipate a major correction of any sort," she said.

Analysts said the market may have gotten a belated boost from news before the opening that consumer prices rose moderately in September, continuing a pattern of tame inflation in a slow-growing economy.
The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index rose 0.3 percent last month after an increase of 0.1 percent in August.
The bond market moved off its lowest level, but the key 30-year Treasury bond ended 7/32 lower, raising its yield to 6.86 percent from 6.84 percent late Tuesday.

In currency markets, the dollar fell to 1.5393 German marks from 1.5410 late Tuesday. It ended little changed at 112.28 Japanese yen. The dollar failed to match Tuesday's high of 112.39, which was its highest level since January of 1994.
Crude oil for November delivery rose then fell $1 but recouped some ground to end 25 cents lower at $25.17 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index fell 26.4 points to 4,024.4. Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 average lost 32.74 points to close at 21,397.19.
